cards.title: Explicit positive-rate codes below the Plotkin point
cards.formal: For every fixed finite adversarial channel \(A\) with rational polyhedral input and noise constraints, and every fixed integer \(L\ge2\), does the existence of a nonconfusable completely positive order-\(L\) distribution with admissible input marginal imply a uniform deterministic polynomial-time encodable family of positive-rate \((L-1)\)-list-decodable codes for that same channel? The alphabets, transition rule, constraints and list bound are fixed as blocklength grows; all terms and the allowed blocklength convention are defined below.
cards.why: The information-theoretic criterion identifies when a channel permits a linear amount of information with a fixed ambiguity bound. Making that criterion explicit would turn a broad existence theorem into efficiently usable encoders without changing the channel or relaxing the list bound.
cards.status_note: Explicit construction is open in the ITCS 2020 source. The 2025 zero-rate theorem and checked 2025 revised derandomization results, including the work published at STOC 2026, do not by their stated guarantees settle this fixed-channel formulation. Later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

importance.reason: This asks whether the general information-theoretic criterion for positive-rate communication against a fixed adversarial channel has an efficient deterministic realization. A universal answer would explain the gap between random existence and explicit error-correcting objects across many channel models while preserving a fixed small list bound.
importance.basis: Individual reading of the ITCS 2020 channel definitions, completely positive achievability criterion and explicit-construction question, with later zero-rate and derandomization results checked for scope.

sentences: A fixed adversarial channel restricts the types of transmitted words and noise words and transforms each input symbol through a specified table.
The source gives a completely positive distribution criterion ensuring that positive-rate codes with a fixed list bound exist.
The question asks whether every channel satisfying that criterion also admits deterministic encoders running in polynomial time in blocklength.
The card fixes a finite-description channel model, preserves its alphabet and list bound, and specifies uniformity and the permitted infinite set of blocklengths.
A resolution would connect a general information-theoretic feasibility criterion with explicit error-correcting constructions across many adversarial channel models.

cards.definitions:
A channel \(A=(X,\Lambda_X,S,\Lambda_S,Y,W)\) has finite alphabets \(X=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(S=\{1,\ldots,b\}\), \(Y=\{1,\ldots,c\}\), where \(a\ge2\) and \(b,c\ge1\). Its deterministic transition rule is a table \(W:X\times S\to Y\). For a finite set \(T\), write \(\Delta(T)=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{T}:\sum_{t\in T}p(t)=1\}\). The nonempty sets \(\Lambda_X\subseteq\Delta(X)\) and \(\Lambda_S\subseteq\Delta(S)\) are closed rational polytopes, each given by finitely many linear equalities and non-strict inequalities with rational coefficients. The table, alphabet sizes, signed integer numerators and positive denominators have ordinary binary encodings. These are fixed channel data, independent of blocklength.

The type of \(u\in T^n\) is \(\tau_u(t)=|\{j:u_j=t\}|/n\). An input word \(x\in X^n\) is admissible if \(\tau_x\in\Lambda_X\). Given \(x\), any \(s\in S^n\) with \(\tau_s\in\Lambda_S\) is allowable noise, and the output is \(y_j=W(x_j,s_j)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). The adversary may choose the entire noise word with knowledge of the entire input word. There is no causality restriction, random channel transition, feedback, shared randomness, insertion or deletion.

A code \(C\subseteq X^n\) consists of admissible input words. It is \((L-1)\)-list-decodable when, for every \(y\in Y^n\), at most \(L-1\) distinct words \(x\in C\) admit an allowable noise word producing \(y\). Different candidate input words may use different noise words. This is a zero-error combinatorial guarantee over every output; it imposes no running-time bound on finding the list.

The promise on \(A,L\) is that there exist a probability vector \(p\in\Lambda_X\), a finite integer \(h\ge1\), probability vectors \(p_1,\ldots,p_h\in\Delta(X)\), and real numbers \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_h\ge0\) with \(\sum_j\lambda_j=1\), such that
\[
Q(x_1,\ldots,x_L)=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_j\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_j(x_i),
\qquad p=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\lambda_jp_j,
\]
is nonconfusable. This is the completely positive distribution condition. The component distributions \(p_j\) need not individually satisfy the input constraints; their common resulting marginal \(p\) must.

Precisely, \(Q\) is confusable if there exists a joint probability distribution \(Z\) on \(X^L\times S^L\times Y\) whose marginal on \(X^L\) is \(Q\), whose \(i\)-th noise-coordinate marginal belongs to \(\Lambda_S\) for every \(1\le i\le L\), and which gives probability one to \(y=W(x_i,s_i)\) simultaneously for all \(i\). Nonconfusable means that no such \(Z\) exists. These distributions are real probability vectors; the promise does not require their entries to be rational or supplied to an encoder.

An explicit positive-rate family means that there exist a rational \(R>0\), an infinite set \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) of blocklengths, two finite deterministic Turing-machine programs \(H,E\), and constants \(K,t\ge1\), with the following properties. On unary input \(1^n\), \(H\) decides whether \(n\in B\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations. For every \(n\in B\), set \(k_n=\lceil Rn\rceil\). On input \((1^n,m)\), with \(m\in\{0,1\}^{k_n}\), the encoder \(E\) outputs \(E_n(m)\in X^n\) in at most \(K(n+1)^t\) bit operations, using binary encodings for output symbols. The map \(E_n\) is injective and its image \(C_n\) is an admissible \((L-1)\)-list-decodable code. Thus the rate \(\log_2|C_n|/n\), measured in information bits per channel use, is at least \(R\).

The programs, constants, rate and infinite length set may depend on the fixed \(A,L\), but not on the particular blocklength or message. Both programs are uniform across lengths and have no advice, oracle, random bits or precomputed codebook supplied as input. The cost bound includes all preprocessing done on that input. No polynomial dependence on the binary description length of a varying channel is required, and there is no demand for a uniform algorithm that produces the programs from the channel. An infinite decidable set of lengths permits divisibility restrictions from exact type constraints; no positive density of those lengths is assumed. The output alphabet is exactly \(X\); replacing it or changing the channel is not allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this universal explicit-construction assertion, including polynomial bit complexity, positive rate and the fixed \((L-1)\) list bound, or a complete Lean proof of its negation for the stated class of channels. A random existence proof, exhaustive construction taking time polynomial only in the exponentially large codebook, or a construction after changing the alphabet does not meet the assertion. Efficient list decoding is not an additional requirement. The asymptotic polynomial-resource and positive-rate requirements do not carry a \(1/100\) numerical tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Section 18, item 4 asks for explicit positive-rate codes whenever a nonconfusable completely positive distribution exists. Theorem 47 already establishes positive-rate existence; the unresolved part is explicit construction.

This card specifies the deterministic finite-alphabet channel branch used in the paper. It explicitly restricts the convex type constraints to fixed closed rational polytopes, so that the channel has finite exact data. It does not claim to cover arbitrary real, length-dependent constraints or stochastic transition rules.

“Explicit” is interpreted as one polynomial-time encoder per fixed channel and list bound, on an infinite polynomial-time recognizable set of lengths. The source’s positive-rate convention permits an infinite sequence of blocklengths. The length-set and Turing-machine clauses make that convention algorithmic, without requiring a code for every length or an efficient list-decoding procedure.

The completely positive condition involves mixtures of independent equal-marginal products. Confusability allows a different noise explanation for each of the candidate codewords, provided that all explanations yield the same output. This is more general than a single Hamming-distance threshold.

The 2025 zero-rate result bounds code size above the list-decoding or list-recovery threshold. Its matching constructions in that regime do not provide positive-rate families for every channel below the threshold.

Later explicit constructions reproduce broad classes of local properties of random linear codes. The checked AEL-based theorem increases the alphabet, and the checked folded Reed–Solomon construction uses an alphabet growing with length. These statements do not by themselves supply codes for every fixed channel and fixed alphabet in this card.

cards.title: Full-length Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond Johnson
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(\varepsilon,\rho\in(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\), a constant \(K\ge1\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and infinitely many prime powers \(q\), such that for every function \(r:\mathbb F_q\to\mathbb F_q\), \[\left|\left\{f\in\mathbb F_q[X]:\deg f\le\lfloor\rho q\rfloor,\;\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb F_q:f(x)=r(x)\}\bigr|>\varepsilon q\right\}\right|\le Kq^c?\] The zero polynomial is included among the degree-bounded polynomials. All four constants are fixed independently of \(q\) and of the received function \(r\). This is the combinatorial full-length Reed–Solomon question from Open Problem 5.20, without a requirement for an efficient decoding algorithm.
cards.why: Reed–Solomon codes are a central algebraic code family, and their list size expresses an intrinsic information limit even when computation is unrestricted. The full-length requirement fixes the evaluation set completely. Determining whether any constant-rate infinite family surpasses the Johnson threshold would resolve a basic distinction between this rigid algebraic family and the punctured variants for which capacity results are known.
cards.status_note: The precise target is open in Vadhan’s 2012 source. The checked 2025 primary papers explicitly distinguish full-length codes from the punctured families covered by their positive results. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the displayed full-length existence statement. This review does not claim that all later parameter regimes or proofs were exhaustively checked.

sentences: The question asks whether some infinite family of full-length Reed–Solomon codes has polynomially bounded lists beyond the Johnson threshold.
The code evaluates every polynomial of degree at most a fixed fraction of the field size at every field element.
One fixed pair of rate and agreement constants and one polynomial list bound must work for every received word along infinitely many field sizes.
This is an information-theoretic existence question and does not demand an efficient decoding algorithm.
Recent capacity theorems for randomly punctured codes and lower bounds for list recovery have different quantifiers or models and do not settle this target.

cards.definitions: A prime power is \(q=p^m\), where \(p\) is a prime and \(m\ge1\) is an integer; the characteristic may vary along the infinite set. The field \(\mathbb F_q\) has exactly \(q\) elements. Let \(d=\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\). The code consists of evaluations of all formal polynomials \(\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jX^j\), with \(a_j\in\mathbb F_q\), at every element of the field. Its block length and alphabet size are both \(q\), its dimension is \(d+1\), and its rate is \((d+1)/q\), which tends to \(\rho\) as \(q\) grows. Because \(d<q\), distinct allowed polynomials give distinct codewords. Coordinates are indexed by field elements, so no ordering choice matters. A received word is an arbitrary function on this entire field and need not be a low-degree polynomial. Its agreement fraction with a codeword is \(q^{-1}|\{x:f(x)=r(x)\}|\); the normalized Hamming distance is one minus this fraction. The displayed list uses strict agreement \(>\varepsilon\), equivalently distance \(<1-\varepsilon\), following the source’s LIST convention. Thus a boundary with exactly \(\varepsilon q\) agreements is excluded. The list is a set of distinct polynomials, not a list with repetitions. The polynomial bound \(Kq^c\) is uniform over all received words and all selected field sizes. Infinitely many prime powers means an unbounded set of distinct values of \(q\); it does not mean every sufficiently large prime power. No efficient method for selecting that infinite set, constructing field representations, finding the list, or encoding its members is required. The evaluation set may not be punctured or replaced by a random proper subset; neither folded symbols, derivatives, restricted message spaces, nor an average over received words is part of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive proof must establish one fixed admissible pair \((\varepsilon,\rho)\), one polynomial list bound and infinitely many field sizes, and the bound must hold for every received word at each of those sizes. It need not supply a decoder. A negative proof must show that for every admissible pair and every \(K\ge1,c\ge1\), only finitely many prime powers have the uniform list bound. Equivalently, beyond a threshold depending on those constants, every prime power must admit some received word with more than \(Kq^c\) qualifying polynomials. Hard instances for only one rate, one characteristic, or an infinite but not exhaustive subsequence do not by themselves refute the existence statement. Results for randomly punctured codes, list recovery with multiple candidate symbols per coordinate, or only algorithmic hardness do not settle this combinatorial full-length target.

context_blocks.text: Vadhan’s Construction 5.14 defines the full-length code by evaluating every degree-at-most-\(d\) polynomial over the entire field. Definition 5.18 uses strict agreement, and Open Problem 5.20 asks for fixed \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\) with degree \(\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\) and polynomial list size along an infinite sequence. The rate convention differs slightly from writing the degree as the dimension.

The Johnson bound and the algorithms recalled in the textbook provide the familiar square-root threshold. The open question asks whether some fixed constant parameters can do strictly better at the level of list cardinalities, including with inefficient decoding.

The 2025 joint journal paper of Alrabiah, Guo, Guruswami, Li and Zhang establishes capacity results for randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes over fields whose sizes are linear in the block length. “Linear-sized” does not mean equal to the block length. Theorem 1.1 explicitly requires a field size strictly greater than the block length when the dimension is positive, so it does not apply to the full-length codes here.

That paper’s introduction distinguishes combinatorial obstructions for some full-length parameter regimes, due to Ben-Sasson, Kopparty and Radhakrishnan, from the later positive puncturing results. A restriction in some regimes does not refute the present existence quantifiers over parameters and infinitely many field sizes.

Li and Shagrithaya’s 2025 paper addresses list recovery, where each received coordinate may specify several acceptable symbols. Its discussion of full-length Reed–Solomon lower bounds concerns that stronger task. Ordinary list decoding here has exactly one received symbol at each coordinate.

cards.title: Polyhedrality of linear-rank inequality cones
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge6\), is the cone \(L_n\) of linear rank inequalities valid over every commutative field polyhedral? Equivalently, for each fixed \(n\ge6\), do finitely many valid coefficient vectors generate every universally valid homogeneous linear inequality on the dimensions of all nonempty sums of \(n\) subspaces by nonnegative real linear combination? The finite generating family may depend on \(n\); no common bound on its size as \(n\) varies is assumed.
cards.why: Dimensions of subspace sums describe the information profiles available to linear coding and linear secret-sharing systems. Finite generation would give a finite complete system of universal linear constraints for each fixed number of subspaces. Nonpolyhedrality would show an intrinsic need for infinitely many constraints even after that number is fixed.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked 2022 seminar Problem (4.4). The complete five-variable result does not extend to all n>=6, and the checked scope of later 2025 work on rank inequalities does not settle polyhedrality. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

importance.reason: The geometry of linear-rank inequality cones controls the possible linear information profiles.
importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: Linear rank inequalities constrain the dimensions of every nonempty sum in a collection of subspaces.
The target cone contains the coefficient vectors of inequalities valid over every commutative field.
The question asks whether this cone is polyhedral for each fixed number of subspaces at least six.
A finite description is known through five subspaces, while increasing families of inequalities for larger collections do not themselves settle the fixed-dimension question.
A resolution would determine whether linear information profiles admit a finite complete set of universal linear constraints at each fixed arity.

cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\mathcal S_n=\{S\subseteq[n]:S\ne\varnothing\}\). A subspace arrangement consists of a commutative field \(F\), a nonnegative integer \(m\), and subspaces \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\) of \(F^m\). Finite and infinite fields, every characteristic, arbitrary ambient dimension, repeated subspaces and the zero subspace are all allowed. Its rank vector \(r\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal S_n}\) has coordinate \(r_S=\dim_F(\sum_{i\in S}V_i)\), where the sum denotes the linear span of the listed subspaces and each finite dimension is embedded in \(\mathbb R\).

A real vector \(a=(a_S)_{S\in\mathcal S_n}\) is a universally valid linear rank inequality if \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_n}a_Sr_S\ge0\) for every such arrangement, including every choice of \(F\). Define \(L_n\) to be the set of all these coefficient vectors. All inequalities are homogeneous and non-strict; no additive constant, normalization, integrality constraint on coefficients or restriction to a fixed characteristic is included. The empty-set coordinate is omitted because its dimension is always zero. In particular \(L_n\) is a closed convex cone in the finite-dimensional real vector space \(\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\).

Here a cone is polyhedral if it is the intersection of finitely many closed homogeneous real halfspaces. For \(L_n\), this is equivalent to finite generation: there exist a nonnegative integer \(M_n\) and vectors \(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(M_n)}\in L_n\) such that
\[
L_n=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{M_n}\lambda_j a^{(j)}:\lambda_j\in\mathbb R,\ \lambda_j\ge0\right\}.
\]
The empty sum is zero. These generators may have arbitrary real coordinates. No effective procedure for finding them, rationality of a generating family or computational bound is requested.

For clarity, the coefficient cone \(L_n\) is the dual of the closed conic hull \(C_n\) of all rank vectors: \(C_n\) is the Euclidean closure of the set of all finite nonnegative real combinations of arrangement vectors, allowing different fields for different arrangements. Then \(L_n=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in C_n\}\). Polyhedrality of \(C_n\) and \(L_n\) is equivalent. The question does not assert that every point of \(C_n\) is itself the rank vector of one arrangement, or that the unclosed conic hull is already closed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(L_n\) is polyhedral for every integer \(n\ge6\), or a complete Lean proof that \(L_n\) is not polyhedral for at least one fixed integer \(n\ge6\). A positive answer may establish the existence of finite generating families without an efficient construction. A growing number of required inequalities as \(n\) increases does not by itself refute polyhedrality at any fixed \(n\). Neither a result for unrestricted entropy inequalities nor a result confined to one field characteristic settles the stated all-fields target by itself.

context_blocks.text: Problem (4.4), attributed to Alexander Shen in the 2022 seminar report, asks about the inequality cones for \(n\ge6\). This card uses the field-independent convention for linear rank inequalities from the subspace-arrangement literature. The report separately asks about field-size and characteristic dependence in Problem (8.3); those restricted cones are not silently substituted for \(L_n\).

The coefficient cone of valid inequalities and the closed cone of admissible rank profiles are dual objects. Making the closure and dual convention explicit prevents a claim about a discrete set of integer rank vectors from being mistaken for the polyhedrality question.

Dougherty, Freiling and Zeger give a complete finite set of inequalities on five variables, including 24 additional types beyond the Shannon and Ingleton inequalities. Their six-variable discussion gives further inequalities without a complete finite description.

Later work studies additional rank inequalities and distinctions between representability and common-information conditions, including in the broader setting of skew fields. Such results about individual inequalities or proof methods do not alone determine whether the full all-fields cone is polyhedral.

sentences: An entropy region collects all joint-entropy vectors realizable by random variables.
The recorded question concerns approximating its faces using variables with bounded alphabets.
A face can encode equalities or limiting relationships that finite-support approximations may struggle to preserve exactly.
A suitable alphabet bound could make otherwise unbounded information-theoretic optimization more accessible to certified computation.

The saved title does not state which faces, approximation metric, or alphabet dependence are intended, so it remains essential to distinguish approximating a nearby entropy vector from staying on the prescribed face.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.
